utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, this morning at 7.00, I received some really bad news, that the mother of Drago Josipovic died last night. I talked to Mr. Drago Josipovic a couple of minutes ago, and he told me that he would prefer not to be present at the hearing today. Now it is up to the Chamber to decide whether to adjourn or whether we should deal with this in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Susak. First of all, let me convey to Mr. Josipovic on behalf of the Court our condolences for this very sad news, and we are very sorry, and of course it goes without saying that Mr. Josipovic, Drago Josipovic, has the right to leave any time, right away, to have some rest and to think of his mother. So we suggest that we should continue with our hearing, but as I say, Mr. Josipovic can leave any time, either right away or later on. It's for him to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, this actually agrees with what Mr. Josipovic has thought. He wanted to retire, to have some peace and quiet, but the hearing should go on, because he does not want to interfere with the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So it is so decided. So you may leave any time. Before we resume with the hearing, is there any outstanding matter, procedural matter to be discussed? Otherwise, as soon as the witness is in, we will resume the cross-examination by Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Drmic. The Prosecutor will continue with his cross-examination. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Madam Judge. Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Mr. Drmic, yesterday you told us that you were mobilised in mid-March 1993 upon a telephone call by Mario Cerkez. Did you know Mario Cerkez at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just one correction. I was mobilised by Mr. Mario Cerkez in mid-March, but he came to see me in my apartment, personally. It wasn't after a telephone conversation. The man from the Defence Department called me on the phone on the 16th of April and instructed me to leave my building, to get inside of my building. As for whether I knew Mario Cerkez -- that was the question, right? -- I knew him very well, from '87, when I started work in the company, in the factory where he himself worked, and we were on good terms, so to speak. One day he visited me in my apartment -- he had called earlier -- and then, in a relaxed atmosphere, he asked me whether I wanted to work for them at the brigade, whether I wanted to deal with the formation of the brigade and the payroll for the personnel, because he knew what I was qualified for. I thought for a couple of seconds, three or four seconds, to see what I wanted to do. He asked me whether I wanted to do that or not, but then he just laughed and said, "Well, you will be mobilised anyway, whether you want to do it or not." I knew at that time what the situation was in Vitez, because before I was laid off at my company, 15 days before I was mobilised, I didn't have any work, I was in my apartment, but when I went to work, that's some 10 or 15 minutes away on foot from my apartment to the place where I worked, and when we -- as we walked by, we had to pass through a place called Mahala that was between the town and the factory, and that was a purely Muslim area. The last day when I went to work I noticed all of a sudden some bunkers that had cropped up in that area, in the Mahala. They were made of logs and of timber, some kind of shelter for combat operations. I was very shocked that day. I did not know what that was for, all the more so when I realised that the openings that were supposed to be for opening the fire, that they were turned towards the town and not towards Travnik, and that was where we expected the Serbian attacks against our valley. That was when I was surprised, and I was somewhat afraid. I guessed that the war was looming, because in some towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina there had already been conflict between Croats and Muslims, such as in Gornji Vakuf and in Busovaca, and after all, there had been conflicts in Vitez in October 1992, a conflict broke out in Vitez between Croats and Muslims. It lasted for five or six days, and after that, people continued to go to the factory together. They worked as if nothing had happened. So the attack that happened again, we thought that it would again be short-lived, but it turned out differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: According to the explanation you provided yesterday, up until that date in March 1993 when you were mobilised, up until that date you were a reservist?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was at my job. In fact, every person of military age was in the reserve force. All of those people who did their national service were in the records of the Office of Defence, and they were automatically considered to be a part of the reserve force, and if need arises, we are all considered as conscripts. Not just me; every man of military age was in the reserve force. I don't know whether the terminology is all right, whether it fits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, let's try and define the word of "reservist." What were the obligations of a reservist at that time and at that particular location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Our obligation as a conscript was to report to the collection point in case of mobilisation. I was not assigned to any war unit. We had not received any military ID from the new government, because all the records dated back from the former Yugoslavia. We had received some training in school and during our national service, and after doing our national service, we were still considered conscripts because if we received our call-up which was issued by the Defence Department, we were supposed to report to the collection point. But I did not have my assignment. I did not know where I was assigned to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Does a reservist have to go on training at particular times?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They maybe had to do so in the former Yugoslavia, because it was a structured army with 50 years of tradition behind it, and reservists at that time had to undergo exercises from training from time to time, but we in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not undergo any training. We did not have to gather after receiving the summons; nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Does a reservist, and I'm not talking about the former Yugoslavia, I'm talking about Central Bosnia at the time we're interested in, that is to say, late 1992, early 1993, at that time, did a reservist, a member of the Croat Community of Bosnia, did that reservist have at home military equipment or parts of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Nobody had any military equipment or any kind of weapons, apart from those persons who were active military personnel, and that was maybe half a year or a year after the conflict, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What about yourself? Did you have a grade in the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have a rank until that time when I was mobilised, but when I was mobilised, my functional post was the chief of financial service, and in itself, that meant that I had the rank of a Major. That was a high rank. But later on, in the course of the war and after the war, real ranks, your personal rank, was assigned to you. Despite the fact that I had been in the Vitez Brigade for almost a year, I was then reassigned to the 3rd Guards Brigade, which was formed sometime in January/February 1994, and I was on the staff, the command of the Guards Brigade as the advisor for information technology to the commander. According to the structure, that was the rank of Captain. But when I left the army, I wanted to be discharged in September 1994, because I wanted to be involved in some work that I really liked. I wanted to start my private business. I got demobilised from the army, and after that I did not have any military rank any more. It was just during the war. I was at a post which had a particular rank. However, I was never given that rank, neither during the war nor afterwards. So when I received my military ID after the war in 1994, it says that I'm a Private. I think it was, in fact, a bit unfair to me, bearing in mind my qualifications and the length of time that I had spent in service, but it wasn't important to me. So that's how it ended up. Now I have the military ID which lists that I have the rank of a Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The injustice that you referred to, who is responsible for that, the new authorities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that it was just an omission on somebody's part, because when the information was gathered for the assignment of ranks in the Vitez Brigade, I was moving to the Guards Brigade. They probably thought that I would get what I have to get there. When this was happening, this process was going on in the Guards Brigade, I was there from January/February 1994, and when the proposals for ranks were finished, I left the army. After that, simply nobody thought about me. Nobody took my file to correct this mistake. On several occasions, I spoke with some officials, some officials that I knew from the war, but I never put anything in writing, nor did I ask for the rank to be given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: During the war, did you always stay in the offices or did you fight on the front?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the war, I was in the office at all times. I slept virtually every night in my apartment except in those cases when I was the duty officer as a member of the command at the brigade command. Then I would spend those nights in the command building, in the brigade command building. I was not issued any weapons. I did have a pistol that was given to me by my wife's brother. He was a soldier, and he actually got killed in December 1993. So I had that pistol with me during the war, but I never discharged it, nor was I issued with any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd like to get your explanations on a document which was already produced in the court, which is Exhibit D39/2, which is a Defence Exhibit, D39/2. Mr. Witness, as you can see, this document was established on the 24th of April, 1993, signed as Slovamir Sivic, and it reports the names of people who were either killed or wounded in the operations carried out by the Vitez Brigade. I'd like to refer to the bottom corner on the left-hand side. Next to number 7 is the name of Zoran Drmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could the witness put this on the ELMO, because we do not have a copy of this exhibit? That would enable us to follow.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not see the name of Zoran Drmic here. What number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I fail to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the first page. There's a number 7 on the bottom of the first page, in the left-hand corner, Mr. President. There is a number 7, next to which is the name Zoran Drmic. But I realise in some copies there is the bottom of the page that's missing. So I'm going to give to the usher my own copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Indeed, in the copy received there is no such thing as a number 7. We go directly from 6 to 8.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. When we talked about lists yesterday, and about the formation of the brigade, and about the job that I did, on several occasions I mentioned that it is not sufficient to have just the first name and the last name without the date of birth and father's name. That's not sufficient information. In Vitez, to be specific, there are four Zoran Drmics, and I often have some minor problems, so to speak, because my mail is sent to their addresses, I receive their mail, and even when I worked at the company, sometimes the loan repayments were taken from my salary and not from their salary. I know three other Zoran Drmics. I think I know who this is. His father's name is Niko. Now, whether he was born in '63 or '65, I don't know exactly, but his father's name is Niko. That's not me. I was wounded, but that was in 1994, on the 30th of January, 1994. I was wounded with shrapnel. En route from my apartment to the brigade command, a shell fell right in front of me, maybe 20 to 30 metres away. It hit a tree. The tree caught most of the blast, but I was hit by a large shrapnel in my groin, so I was hospitalised. That was at the end of the war. I have all the requisite medical documents. It was declared that I was 20 per cent disabled after that incident. So those lists of the casualties, that refers to the first few days. I know most of the names here because I entered this data into the computer and I kept the records. I recognise some other names. Number 34, that's my friend I talked to you about when I told you what it was like at the front line. That's Goran Martinovic. That was on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now going to talk, Mr. Witness, about the relationships you had with the accused, Vlatko Kupreskic. You said that you met him before the war when you worked together in the same company. At that time did you notice that Vlatko Kupreskic may have health problems or may have a condition that could be annoying him in his daily life?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is correct that I had met Vlatko during the war, because we had our respective offices in the same building. However, we never sat down together or talked, not even for a minute or two. It was just in passing really. We would greet each other, and that was it. Perhaps just to exchange a couple of words, shake hands, because we worked together but we had never spoke about anything else. I had no information that he had any condition, health condition. So I was all the more surprised when he came to my office during the war and gave this document to (redacted), and it was only then that I learned about his health condition. Can I just ask something? This monitor is flickering and this light is bothering me. Can this be turned off, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As a consequence, Mr. Witness, when you met and when you became acquainted with Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic before the war, in the conditions you described, it did not appear that he may have any sort of condition in his daily life?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't seem to me that way, and we did not address that at all. My acquaintance with him was such that I saw him for the first time when I was going to serve in the army. I was 18 at the time, and it was customary to have a feast, and Vlatko Kupreskic played the guitar, and he came with a friend who played accordion. That's when I saw him for the first time. After that, we saw each other infrequently in our company. That is what really bound us, the only thing, because we never sat down, had coffee, talked, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that after the war you entered into a business relationship with Mr. Kupreskic, and that in 1995, for instance, you virtually met him on a daily basis. Can you be more specific as to this business relationship that you had with Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometime in October or November, 1994, he called me on the telephone, myself and a friend of mine, because we had just registered a company which was to provide some bookkeeping services for private businesses. He was setting up his own company, and he wanted to do so bookkeeping research so that he wouldn't have any problems with the authorities. Then we worked with him on that, because his company was growing by the day and becoming more and more successful. So we worked throughout 1995, 1996, '97, and '98. In fact, we still work with them even though he has been absent, but his wife comes to us, and I know all of his workers, all of his -- I know that on his premises he has computers, and I installed for him the programmes for the flow of merchandise. So I know of him, of his business. So he would come to my office frequently, every 10, 15 days, or at least once a month to check how the bookkeeping was going, whether there were any documents missing or any other problems with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that time when you had that business relationship, did the health of Mr. Kupreskic seem to be problematic, according to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It didn't seem problematic to me, even though at that time I had had a different opinion, because I had learned from (redacted) that he had a pacemaker. I was sort of trying to gauge whether that was giving him any problems. I think two or three years later I had -- I finally asked him whether he had a pacemaker, and he said no, that he did not have one but that he had only been operated on his heart, and that (redacted) may have misunderstood that he had a pacemaker. But I could not see that he had any health problems, something that would impede him in his activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that managing a company like the one he was managing required physical abilities, I mean, a major physical ability? In other words, his business, his job was quite an active job and it required him to be in good health?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You could say so, even though not necessarily, because this business may have involved just making phone calls to his business partners, and I think that his workers and his wife may have been involved. Perhaps his wife was keeping all the books and doing the paperwork anyway. In fact, as far as I recall, she was indeed the manager of the company, at least on paper. But I knew that a point of fact, Mr. Vlatko was running the company, that it was due to his activities that the company had survived. Because in this particular segment, business sector -- that is, the wholesale food business -- the competition was very strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could we say, Mr. Witness, that that company managed by Vlatko Kupreskic was, in 1994, '95, '96, a prosperous company which was constantly growing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You could say so, because the company was improving year by year until he went to The Hague, when suddenly the company took a downward turn, and the company posted great losses, and I don't know what its future will be, in other words, how much longer it will be able to go on. Now, this is perhaps a bit confidential. I don't know whether I should reveal any information about this business.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you any more regarding that anyway. Let's go back to the time of the war. You said that the name of Vlatko Kupreskic was in the computer with a marking saying that he was unfit for service. What was the reason that the name "Vlatko Kupreskic" was introduced in the computer if he could not be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The reason was that all lists coming to our office were analysed to great detail, and regardless of the circumstances, each individual was entered in this list, whoever was -- every single person was registered just so that we would have it there. However, when we went into the field, we tried to find out whether this person was actually a member of the brigade or not so that we would able to come up with the actual numbers, who was the member and where they belonged. Later, when the units were -- when everything was broken down into particular units, such as companies, battalions, in the field, we then interviewed each of these individuals, and whoever did not have any kind of code, we would say, "Where does this person belong?" Especially from the southern sector, we would ask the commander, "Where is this person?" And for instance, the commander would say, "Well, he is a member of the company." Then we would enter his wartime assignment. If the commander said, "He is not part of the unit," or "He is unfit," we would just enter that, because we could not trace everybody. It was the commander's word which we had to rely on, and we just had to take it for granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As a consequence, Mr. Witness, if the name "Vlatko Kupreskic" was entered in your computer, it is that it was on a list which you copied?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. I believe that that was the list which we saw yesterday. That is the exhibit provided by the Defence. I think that that was the list sent to us, and then these may have been actually the first lists which we had at our disposal. However, at that time, we did not know which individual was in which unit. I mentioned that there was this date of birth and father's name. We did not know the location of each and every soldier. These were just the initial lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you please remind us of what lists you are presently talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had a list here yesterday. It was signed by Marijan Skopljak, and the heading was from the Defence Department. It was some kind of report on mobilisation which I believe the head of the office had sent to someone in order to let those people know that he had done something. I don't know who compiled these lists, whether they are authentic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, that list holds the date, unless I'm mistaken, 22nd or 23rd of April, 1993. Are you saying that the name "Vlatko Kupreskic" was not introduced in your computer and in your logs until that date, the 22nd or 23rd of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I recall from yesterday, that list was dated 29 April, and until that date we practically had no records in our computers. So these were just the initial -- that was the starting point. We only had more complete lists in the course of the months of May and June and so on. But early on, that is, in April, these people who were in this list, we did not have them on record, because we only had the active part of these units entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you told us yesterday that in September '93, Vlatko Kupreskic was sent before you -- or came before (redacted), but at any rate, you were there -- and he was shown in by two policemen wearing uniforms in order to receive an assignment. And you said that you had a very precise recollection of that scene, as if it happened yesterday. Could you explain why this scene was so striking to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was striking to me how (redacted) addressed me and looked at me in a strange way. She was perhaps a bit angry, and she said, "See? See what they are doing to me?" And I looked at her questioningly, not realising what she was trying to say, so I asked, "What is this all about?" She said, "Well, they are bringing to me these unfit people and asking me to mobilise them and to place them somewhere. What am I going to do with him?" Then she said, "I'm putting him in a medical unit as a driver." So I remember it more by the reaction of (redacted), but I do know that it related to Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. Had it been some other circumstances, had (redacted) not reacted the way she did, I may not have remembered it, because we had frequent cases that people -- these people would be brought to us. I think that this was during the most fierce fighting in our valley, at the time we when were suffering the greatest losses, and then the order from the command was that basically nobody would be considered unfit, that everybody should be involved in the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said yesterday, Mr. Witness, that in the circumstances prevailing at the time when the enemy would attack, everybody was supposed to bring in his contribution to the measure of his skills and as far as they could. As far as you know, what was the contribution brought in by Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic in the defence effort from April '93 and September '93 date at which you met him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I do not know that. I did not see him during that period, nor did I see him in the period just prior to the war, so I do not know in what way he was engaged. I don't know if he even was engaged. I only know that as far as the computer is concerned, his name existed there, but he did not have any assignment. It was not clear whether he had been assigned to some battalion company, squad, or -- at the time when he had been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For things to be perfectly clear on this point, Mr. Witness, what you're reporting is that the computer does not say anything in this regard, and besides, you have no particular recollection regarding the action by Mr. Kupreskic at the time, and I'm referring to the period April to September 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. At that time, in that spirit, I did not see Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, nor do I know what kind of activities he was engaged in, what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, before this Court, in previous circumstances, we heard that according to the texts applicable in the HVO, mobilisation could be either public or secret, partial or complete, in full. In light of your experience and in your functions at the time, could you explain what a secret mobilisation involved?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN DRMIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could not, because I hear these things for the first time, and my function was really to just process these lists. The data in the computer were available at all times, and I could produce any type of list in five minutes. So had it not been for the computers, I don't know what kind of information we would have been able to produce at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Terrier. Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions. Mr. Drmic, thank you for coming to The Hague to give evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina, shall we now call witness number 3, Court witness? Any protective measures? Oh, Mr. Par will be conducting the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness has asked for closed session, because it is a witness of another ethnicity who is afraid that his testimony here may involve some consequences for him. Although perhaps the content of his testimony does not warrant this, it is his personal request, and he has requested that this be conducted in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will comply with this request. Let us now move into a closed session then, and then we will bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: at 1.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of May, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
